newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI seen holding lower house.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI seen holding lower house.

text.p: Mexico's electoral system favours the all-powerful Institutional Revolutionary Party's retaining control of the lower house of Congress after this year's mid-term polls, a veteran Mexico watcher said.

But victory by the opposition National Action Party (PAN) in the race for mayor of Mexico City could substantially change the country's political panorama, said John Bailey, professor of government and director of the Mexico project at Georgetown University in Washington.
Bailey was in Mexico to launch a book of which he is co-editor, "Strategic and security issues in U.S.-Mexican relations: Beyond the Cold War."

Mexico will hold elections on July 6 for the lower house Chamber of Deputies and one-quarter of the Senate. Many political analysts see PRI waging an uphill battle to retain control of the lower house in the wake of a severe economic crisis and political scandals since the last elections were held in 1994.
Bailey said in an interview that the PRI's traditional trump card -- exploiting fears of alternative government -- may have weakened, but the playing field was still slanted in its favour.
Out of a total of 500 seats up for grabs in the Chamber of Deputies, 300 are for single-member districts where a party does not need to gain an overall majority to win.
"All you need is 30 percent of the vote, with four parties running, to win it. So the short of it is, I would be very surprised if the PRI lost control of the lower house," Bailey said.

"With 300 single-member districts it's easy for the hegemonic party to play off oppositions... Even if the PRI were to drop below that 50-percent threshold they would still be the majority, the paralysis party, in a three-party coalition," he added.

Voters this year will also choose the mayor of Mexico City, who has been directly appointed by the president since 1929. Recent opinion polls suggest that a direct race in the capital could be won by the PAN.
Bailey said an opposition victory in Mexico City would change "the expectations of political actors throughout the system, that the future can be very different."
"The problems of fracturing, of people deserting, that you see in the PRI would be multiplied in ways that are hard to imagine...you could see the disintegration of the PRI," he said.
In short, the end was in sight of what he called "a system held together for so long by a hegemonic party and opposition parties that are trying to gain ground."

Bailey said the PRI was still a "hegemonic" party as it still had the ability to modify rules to serve its own interests, he said. The PRI has held the presidency and a majority of both houses of Congress since it was founded in 1929.
Much still depends, however, on how the PAN could face the many pitfalls of running Mexico City, Bailey said.
Bailey said a PAN mayor, for example, could have trouble justifying the capital's usual "lion's share of federal funds" to PAN provincial governors who have long sought a fairer share.
"I don't think PAN wants to think about those things. I think what they're going to do is win, and then see what happens next," he said.
